item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 837 as two die in 24 hours
item.description:
Two more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 837.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified both of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 741, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 96, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Of the two new suspected fatalities, one was reported in the Sylhet division and the other in the Barisal division.
A total of 900 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 128,310.
During the same period, 185 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 16,059.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 110,987 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 106,859 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Bomb concealed inside pressure cooker recovered, defused in Savar
item.description:
A bomb concealed inside a pressure cooker was recovered from an abandoned bag at a tea stall in Ashulia of Savar and later neutralized in a controlled explosion by the Bomb Disposal Unit of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) on Friday morning.
According to police and local residents, the abandoned bag was spotted around 11pm on Thursday in front of Joyi General Store, a tea stall owned by Hridoy Chakma in the Khejur Bagan area of Ashulia. As the bag remained unattended for a long time, locals became suspicious.
Ashulia Police Station Officer-in-Charge Tarikul Islam said: "An investigation has begun to identify and arrest those involved."
"At the same time, CCTV footage from the surrounding area is being collected and analyzed," he said.
After opening the bag, locals found a bomb concealed inside a pressure cooker and immediately informed police.
Personnel from Ashulia Police Station rushed to the scene, cordoned off the area, and initially determined the object to be an explosive before referring the matter to the DMP Bomb Disposal Unit.
Bomb disposal personnel recovered the explosive device and took it to a vacant plot inside Amir Sarkar's Housing, adjacent to United Garments on Bangabandhu Road in Ashulia Union, where it was safely neutralized through a controlled explosion.
The incident triggered panic among residents in the area.
"We did not initially pay much attention after noticing the bag in front of the shop at night. However, after becoming suspicious and checking the bag, we found the bomb and immediately informed the police," said local resident Azizul Haque.
He said they believed their prompt action helped avert a possible major accident.

item.title: The world’s oldest epic gets a blockbuster retelling
item.description:
The countdown to one of Indian cinema’s most ambitious films has officially begun.
The makers of Ramayana: Part 1 unveiled the long-awaited trailer on Wednesday, offering audiences their most extensive look yet at Nitesh Tiwari’s epic retelling of the ancient Hindu mythological saga.
Released simultaneously in five Indian languages -- Hindi, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Malayalam -- the trailer introduces a world where gods, mortals and demons collide in a battle that will determine the fate of the universe.
The story begins with the Hindu trinity -- Brahma the creator, Vishnu the protector and Shiva the transformer -- watching over the three realms of existence.
As chaos engulfs heaven and earth, Vishnu descends to the mortal world as Rama, played by Ranbir Kapoor, the righteous prince of Ayodhya destined to restore cosmic balance.
Standing in his way is Ravana, portrayed by Kannada superstar Yash.
Blessed with extraordinary power and driven by pride and vengeance, the immortal king of Lanka declares dominion over heaven, earth and the underworld, setting the stage for an inevitable confrontation between two of mythology’s most enduring figures.
The trailer traces Rama’s transformation from the beloved heir to Ayodhya’s throne into the reluctant hero of an epic destiny.
Alongside his devoted wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) and loyal brother Lakshman (Ravie Dubey), Rama’s peaceful life is shattered when exile and Ravana’s abduction of Sita push him towards a war that will shape the destinies of gods and mortals alike.
Visually, the trailer embraces spectacle at every turn.
Towering palaces, celestial landscapes and sprawling battlefields are brought to life through lavish production design and cutting-edge visual effects, while large-scale action sequences hint at the epic scale the filmmakers are aiming to achieve.
Director Nitesh Tiwari appears to be balancing mythological grandeur with emotional storytelling, while the first footage showcases an ambitious blend of mythology, fantasy and blockbuster filmmaking.
Produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios in collaboration with eight-time Academy Award-winning visual effects studio DNEG and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations, Ramayana: Part 1 ranks among the most expensive and technically ambitious productions ever mounted in Indian cinema.
The film is scheduled for a worldwide release during Diwali 2026, with Sony Pictures handling international distribution and Dharma Productions distributing the film across North India.

item.title: Info minister: No religion-based conspiracy to succeed
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon on Friday said no conspiracy based on religion or race will be allowed to succeed in Bangladesh, warning against attempts to exploit people's religious beliefs for political or other gains.
“If any quarter tries to exploit religious belief and religious practices to bring people under its influence, ordinary people will identify them. No conspiracy based on religion or race will be allowed to succeed in Bangladesh,” he said.
The minister was speaking as the chief guest at the biennial conference of the Barisal district unit of the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad at the Barisal District Shilpakala Academy.
He referred to Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman’s stance that religion belongs to individuals, while the state belongs to everyone.
Swapon said any attempt to capture the state in the name of religion or to use followers of any faith for political purposes amounts to communalism and runs contrary to the principles of religion.
"Whenever any group tries to turn religious belief and practice into a tool of communal politics, devout people themselves will identify those who exploit religion for personal or political gain," he added.
The minister also said political leaders should always work for the welfare of the people.
"As long as people believe that a political party's activities serve their interests, they will continue to support that party and its election symbol," he said.
Barisal City Corporation Administrator Advocate Bilkis Akter Jahan Shirin and Barisal Zila Parishad Administrator Akon Quddusur Rahman, among others, were present with Manik Lal Mukharjee, president of the district unit of the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad, in the chair.

item.title: Sergio Gor visits Rohingya camps in Cox's Bazar
item.description:
US President Donald Trump's Special Envoy for South and Central Asia and US ambassador to India Sergio Gor visited the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox's Bazar on Friday to assess the humanitarian situation of displaced Myanmar nationals.
The 11-member delegation arrived at Cox's Bazar airport at 11:55 am before travelling directly to the Rohingya camps in Ukhiya. The delegation also included the US ambassador to Bangladesh Brent Christensen.
According to the Office of the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC), the delegation inspected the World Food Programme's (WFP) humanitarian operations at Camp 4 in Ukhiya. The itinerary also included visits to Extended Camp 8 West (8W) and Camp 6.
During the visit, the delegation observed the living conditions of the Rohingya refugees, ongoing humanitarian assistance programmes and the overall conditions in the camps. They are also expected to review the activities of humanitarian agencies working there.
The delegation is scheduled to meet officials at the RRRC office in Cox's Bazar at 5:00 pm to exchange views on the Rohingya response.
Gor arrived in Dhaka on Thursday on a three-day official visit. His trip is scheduled to conclude on Saturday with a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

item.title: Patient dies after jumping from DMCH building
item.description:
A patient died after jumping from the eighth floor of the new building at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) early Friday.
The deceased was identified as Riya Begum, a resident of Bhadurdangi village in Pabna Sadar upazila.
She was rushed to the hospital's emergency department after the incident, where the on-duty doctor declared her dead.
Riya's father, Latif Mallik, said she had been admitted to Ward 802 of the hospital's Medicine Department three days earlier.
"Early in the morning, relatives of another patient alerted me that my daughter was about to jump from the balcony. I ran towards her, but before I could reach her, she jumped. Everyone tried to stop her, but she did not listen," he said.
According to Latif, Riya landed on the roof of a parked private car before being taken to the emergency department.
He said Riya had married a Bangladeshi expatriate living in Singapore around four and a half years ago. Her husband returned to Singapore about two years ago after visiting Bangladesh.
Latif also said Riya had been suffering from mental health problems, which had worsened over the past 10 days.
Inspector Md Faruk of the DMCH police outpost said the body had been kept at the hospital morgue and Shahbagh police station had been informed.

item.title: Three held with 464 weapons at Baitul Mukarram
item.description:
Police arrested three people and seized a large cache of locally made weapons and other equipment during a special drive at Link Road adjacent to the Baitul Mukarram Gold Market in the capital on Thursday.
The arrestees were identified as Robiul Islam, 40, Md Azad, 30, and Md Rajan, 34.
Harun Or Rashid, deputy commissioner of the Motijheel Division of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), said the operation was launched to curb the illegal sale of sharp weapons used in muggings, violent crimes and other criminal activities in the capital.
During the raid, police recovered a total of 464 weapons and related items, including machetes, large knives, switchblade knives, combat knives, electric stun guns, Chinese axes, baton sticks and toy pistols designed to resemble real firearms.
According to preliminary interrogation, the seized weapons and equipment had been stockpiled for sale to individuals involved in criminal activities across different parts of the capital.

item.title: DNCC administrator vows action against unfit vehicles, unskilled drivers
item.description:
Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) Administrator Md Safiqul Islam Khan on Friday said strict legal action will be taken against unfit vehicles and unlicensed or unskilled drivers in coordination with the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA).
He made the remarks while visiting the house of DNCC conservancy worker Shefali Begum, who was killed in a road accident while on duty in the Madhya Badda area earlier in the day.
After learning of the tragic road accident, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman instructed the authorities to immediately visit the residence of the deceased sanitation worker.
Following the directive, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Mir Shahe Alam, State Minister for Housing and Public Works Ahammad Sohel Monzoor and the DNCC administrator rushed to the victim's home.
Safiqul said action will also be taken against anyone found driving DNCC vehicles without proper skills or if any helper is found driving a vehicle after an investigation.
He said conservancy workers work day and night to keep the city clean and urged everyone to ensure their safety while performing their duties.
The DNCC announced Tk4 lakh in financial assistance and one year’s salary for Shefali’s family.
The administrator expressed condolences to the bereaved family and called on reckless drivers to exercise caution to prevent road accidents.
DNCC Chief Waste Management Officer Commodore Mohammad Humayun Kabir and other officials were present during the visit.

item.title: Thousands cross into Spain’s north Africa enclave in new migrant crisis
item.description:
Thousands of migrants crossed overnight from Morocco into Spain’s north Africa’s Ceuta enclave as Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday arrived to manage one the largest migrant crisis on the country’s border.
In recent days, a total of around 40,000 migrants have crossed into the territory, a police source said, many swimming around the small border barrier that meets with the Mediterranean sea.
The sudden massive influx has sparked an international crisis for Spain’s government, drawing criticism from Italy and Finland and prompting France to tighten checks on its border with Spain.
Madrid has sent troops and more police, including divers, drones and boats, to boost security in Ceuta. Sanchez and his interior minister arrived on Friday to visit the enclave’s Tarajal border.
AFP reporters have seen hundreds of people -- men, women and children -- entering Ceuta by swimming around a border barrier with Morocco to enter the Spanish exclave, discarding flotation rings and clothes used in the risky passage.
On Friday, hundreds of migrants mostly young men were hanging around near the border and in the town while others were turning back to Morocco, saying “there are too many people here.”
So far, 18 people have died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave, the police source said.
“There was a steady stream of people all night long,” the source said, adding that migrants “continued to arrive overnight and are still arriving” early Friday.
It was not immediately clear what has prompted the recent surge of migrants from Morocco.
In 2021, thousands crossed to take advantage of Rabat loosening border controls during a diplomatic dispute with Spain.
Already the Ceuta scenes of the surge in migrants were causing diplomatic fallout.
Italy on Thursday called for Spain to be suspended from Europe’s open-borders Schengen zone, prompting Spain to summon Italy’s ambassador and accuse Rome of using the crisis for political gain.
Finland on Friday also backed Italy’s call to shut Spain out of the zone over the crisis.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X that he had “given instructions to immediately step up controls at the Spanish border” on Thursday night.
Two top officials within US President Donald Trump’s White House on Thursday also reiterated their anti-immigration politics using video of Ceuta.
Ceuta, a territory of 18.5 square kilometers (seven square miles), and similar enclave Melilla have Europe’s only two land borders with Africa.
Ebullient migrants on Thursday were walking through the streets of Ceuta, thanking the Spanish police and calling out: “Bye bye Morocco, hello Spain.”
Police and Civil Guards in Ceuta appeared to do little to intervene, although some officers attempted to direct the arrivals to the local migrant reception center.
Morocco’s authorities had not yet issued an official statement on the flow of migrants, but a Moroccan official source told AFP on condition of anonymity that the two countries had spoken about the matter.
In 2021, more than 10,000 migrants reached Ceuta from neighboring Morocco over the course of two days, taking advantage of a loosening of border controls by Rabat during a crisis between the two countries.
That dispute erupted after Spain decided to host the leader of the Sahrawi independence movement, the Polisario Front, for medical treatment.
Polisario guerillas fought a long war with Morocco over independence of the Western Sahara region. Morocco’s neighbor Algeria had supported the Polisario group.
That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its long-standing policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara-- a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Madrid and Algiers.
Sanchez visited Algiers on July 20 -- the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years -- marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.

item.title: Rancon, MG JW Pakistan sign MoU for vehicle exports
item.description:
Pakistan's MG JW Automobile and Bangladesh's Rancon Group have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) for the export of vehicles from Pakistan to Bangladesh, according to a press release issued by the Pakistan High Commission in Dhaka.
Under the agreement, 100 vehicles will be exported to Bangladesh this year, according to Pakistan's Ministry of Industries and Production. Total exports are projected to reach 5,800 vehicles over the next four years.
The partnership is expected to expand the range of vehicles available in Bangladesh's market, promote competition, and provide consumers with more choices at competitive prices. It is also expected to strengthen economic cooperation between Pakistan and Bangladesh and encourage greater business-to-business collaboration, the release said.
Rancon Group Executive Director Muhammad Mostafizur Rashid Bhuiyan said the agreement would introduce greater competition in Bangladesh's automobile market while providing consumers with high-quality vehicles manufactured in Pakistan.
Pakistan's Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Industries and Production, Haroon Akhtar Khan, welcomed the agreement and said such partnerships would strengthen trade and economic ties between Pakistan and Bangladesh and create new opportunities for cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.
The signing ceremony was attended by senior officials of both companies, government representatives, and members of the business community, the release added.

item.title: PM Tarique Rahman drives through Dhaka to inspect city cleanliness
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Friday personally drove through different roads under the Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) to inspect the city’s cleanliness as part of his government efforts to make Dhaka a cleaner capital, news agency BSS report.

“The Prime Minister personally drove through different roads in the northern part of the capital this afternoon to see the cleanliness situation on the ground. His vehicle crossed Shyamoli around 6:10 pm,” said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony.

The Prime Minister left his Gulshan residence at 4:05 pm and drove the vehicle himself, Rony added.

Rony said the Prime Minister has repeatedly stated that he wants to see Dhaka as a clean city. That is why he was personally touring the city roads to inspect the cleanliness situation, he added.

Our correspondent reports: During the inspection, the prime minister's motorcade travelled through ECB Chattar, Mirpur DOHS, Diabari, Uttara Sectors 3, 4, 5 and 6, Airport Road, Kakoli intersection, Mohakhali, Farmgate, Manik Mia Avenue, Asad Gate, Salimullah Road, Iqbal Road, Tajmahal Road and Japan Garden City in Mohammadpur, Shyamoli intersection, Ganabhaban intersection, Zia Udyan, Shewrapara, Kazipara, Mirpur-10, Kachukhet, Cantonment, Sainik Club, Kakoli and Banani. After completing the inspection, he returned to his residence on Gulshan Avenue in the evening.

According to BSS, State Minister for LGRD and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, DNCC Administrator Md. Safiqul Islam Khan Milton, BNP Special Secretary Belayet Hossain, PM’s Private Secretary Md. Mehedul Islam and Assistant Private Secretary Abdur Rahman Suny accompanied the Prime Minister in the vehicle.

item.title: Those who want people to forget 1971 never believe in Bangladesh: Mirza Fakhrul
item.description:
"I always say one thing: those who want people to forget 1971, or make them forget it, actually never believe in Bangladesh. Because if we are to believe in Bangladesh, we must keep 1971 at the forefront. We will move forward with that," Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) Secretary General and Local Government Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir said on Friday.

Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir made these remarks while addressing a discussion with leaders of the Hindu community as the chief guest today, Friday, at the Institution of Diploma Engineers auditorium in Kakrail, Dhaka.

The discussion and representatives' conference, titled "Ensuring the Protection and Security of Minorities," was organised by the Sammilita Sanatan Parishad.

Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir said that keeping 1971 at the forefront does not mean pushing the July mass uprising of 2024 into the background. Rather, along with 1971, July must also be remembered.

He said, "We cannot deny July either. Countless of our sons sacrificed their lives to establish democracy in Bangladesh. They forced a fascist government to leave the country."

The BNP secretary general further said the party does not regard either 1971 or 2024 as less important than the other.

Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir alleged that a certain group is deliberately trying to push the country towards division in the name of religion.

He said those attempting to divide the country in the name of religion must be resisted.

"We cannot allow extremism here. We cannot allow fundamentalism. We want to build a liberal, democratic Bangladesh," he stated.

Warning those who seek to create division in the name of religion, Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir called for resisting extremism and fundamentalism. He said people of all faiths enjoy equal rights in Bangladesh. The BNP does not regard anyone as a "minority," he said, urging followers of the Sanatan faith to remain vocal in asserting their rights.

Thanking members of the Sanatan community for supporting the BNP in the last parliamentary election, Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir said the party and the future government would sincerely work to address their various problems.

He requested representatives of the Hindu community to maintain communication and dialogue with the BNP.

The event was inaugurated by Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury. He said minority votes had played an important role in bringing the BNP to power this time. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also remembers that support with gratitude, he said.

The government considers all citizens equal. Hindus, Buddhists, Christians and people of any faith will enjoy equal rights. The BNP government is committed to protecting those rights, he added.

Prime Minister's Special Assistant Bijon Kanti Sarkar stressed the importance of presenting impartial and accurate information without bias when analysing any situation.

He said political and social contexts should be assessed not only by looking at the past year or two but by considering the entire historical background.

Speakers at the event said that when crimes occur, they should not be viewed solely as attacks on a particular community but assessed in the context of the overall situation.

They also noted that discrepancies in data provided by different organisations create difficulties for the government in making decisions. They therefore called for the publication of unified and accurate information to avoid confusion.

Sammilita Sanatan Parishad General Secretary Pradip Kumar Acharya moderated the event with its President Professor Hirendranath Biswas in the chair.

Among others, Mymensingh-8 lawmaker Lutfullahel Majed, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister's Office ABM Abdus Sattar, Hindu Religious Welfare Trust Vice Chairman Tapan Chandra Majumdar and senior lawyer Subrata Chowdhury also addressed the meeting.

Ashok Taru Saha, representing 46 organisations of minority communities, presented the keynote address.

He alleged that attacks on the Hindu community had recently increased to a level higher than at any other time. He urged the government to immediately play a stronger role in protecting the rights of minority communities.

During the discussion, the Sammilita Sanatan Parishad placed several demands before the government. These included establishing a Ministry of Minority Affairs and a National Minority Commission, ensuring justice for attacks and persecution against minority communities, granting appropriate government holidays for Hindu religious festivals, allocating government land and providing necessary support to the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust, and upgrading the trust into a foundation.

item.title: Police defuse ‘pressure cooker’ bomb found in bag left at grocery shop in Ashulia
item.description:
Police have recovered a specially constructed improvised explosive device (IED) from a travel bag left at a grocery shop in Ashulia, Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka.

The device was later safely defused by the Bomb Disposal Unit of the police’s Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) Division.

According to Ashulia police station, at around 9:30 pm on Thursday, a man wearing a face mask entered a grocery shop in the Charabag area of Ashulia to buy a soft drink. He handed the shopkeeper a Tk200 note to pay for his purchase. As the shopkeeper did not have sufficient change, he went to an adjacent shop to exchange the note. When he returned, the customer had disappeared, leaving behind a locked travel bag.

Police said that after waiting for a considerable time without the man returning to collect the bag, the shopkeeper informed local residents. When the bag was opened, they found a pressure cooker wrapped in Scotch tape. Suspecting it to be hazardous, they alerted Ashulia police station. Police officers arrived at the scene, cordoned off the area and carried out an initial inspection. They confirmed that the tape-wrapped pressure cooker contained explosive materials and immediately informed senior officials.

At around 6:30 am on Friday, after securing the surrounding area, the CTTC Bomb Disposal Unit transported the device to a nearby open field, where it was safely defused.

Mohammad Tariqul Islam, Officer-in-Charge of Ashulia police station, said a case had been filed under the Explosive Substances Control Act.

He told Prothom Alo that efforts were under way to identify and arrest the individual who left the travel bag at the shop.

Rape, suicide rise in July despite decline in overall violence against women: MSF
item.description:
Although the overall number of incidents of violence against women and children declined slightly in July compared to June, cases of rape and suicide increased during the month.

Rights body Manabadhikar Shongskriti Foundation (MSF) disclosed the data in a monthly report on gender-based violence. According to its statistics, rape cases rose by nearly 33 per cent in July, while suicides increased by about 65 per cent.

The findings were released in a press statement sent to the media today, Friday, signed by MSF President Sultana Kamal. The report was prepared based on information published in several leading national newspapers and data provided by local human rights activists.

MSF recorded 320 incidents of violence against women and children across the country in June. The number fell to 306 in July. Although the overall number of incidents declined by about 4.4 per cent, the organisation described the situation as still alarming.

According to its assessment, while the total number of reported crimes has decreased, the nature of the violence has become increasingly brutal and complex.

Alarming rise in rape and suicide

MSF's statistics show that 90 rape cases were reported in July, compared to 68 in June, representing an increase of nearly 33 per cent in just one month. Incidents of sexual harassment or abuse also increased slightly, rising from 21 cases in June to 22 in July.

Meanwhile, 17 suicides were reported in June, but the number rose to 28 in July—an increase of nearly 65 per cent within a month.

MSF believes that the increase in rape cases indicates an acute sense of insecurity among women and children. The high rate of suicide, it says, may reflect the psychological consequences of social oppression and impunity.

Some forms of crimes declined

Despite the rise in rape and suicide, several indicators of violence declined during July. Gang rape cases fell from 16 in June to seven in July. Cases involving both rape and murder declined from five to three. Attempted rape cases dropped slightly from 35 to 34.

Incidents of physical assault fell from 56 in June to 42 in July.

In addition, 76 women and children were victims of murder in June, while the figure declined to 52 in July. However, incidents of abduction and disappearance increased slightly, from 12 to 13. As in June, one acid attack was reported in July.

Settlement of criminal offences through arbitration and recovery of abandoned newborns

MSF expressed deep concern over the continuing practice of settling serious criminal offences through informal arbitration (shalish) in violation of the law.

According to the report, at least three cases involving attempted rape and sodomy were settled through illegal arbitration in July. Of these, two were cases of attempted rape, while one was a case of sodomy.

The report also documented the recovery of 11 abandoned newborns during July. Among them, eight were found dead, while three were rescued alive.

According to the report, police generally fail to conduct effective investigations to identify those responsible in such cases, allowing perpetrators to remain beyond the reach of the law.

In cases involving deceased newborns, police usually file unnatural death cases, while surviving infants are handed over to the Department of Social Services.

According to MSF, the practices of illegal arbitration and newborn abandonment further reinforce a culture of impunity in society.

Health minister pledges support for Thalassemia patients
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Friday said the government will provide the highest level of support to thalassemia patients.
He said this while addressing the Blood Donor Recognition 2026 ceremony organized by the Bangladesh Thalassemia Samity (BTS) at the Institution of Engineers, Bangladesh (IEB) in Ramna in the capital.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s spouse and Ziaur Rahman Foundation Vice-President and renowned cardiologist Dr Zubaida Rahman attended the event as the chief guest.
The event was arranged to recognize and express gratitude to voluntary blood donors for their invaluable contributions.
Highlighting the contributions of blood donors, the health minister described repeated blood donations to save patients' lives as a noble humanitarian initiative.
One young donor who donated blood 41 times for thalassemia patients, while another donated 38 times, were recognized today.
Recalling the healthcare vision of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, Sakhawat said whenever Ziaur Rahman traveled to villages across the country, he took doctors with him.
He also encouraged people to adopt healthier food habits to raise public awareness, improve lifestyles, and build a healthier nation.
Emphasizing the importance of disease prevention, the minister said that critical illnesses-including cancer, kidney disease, and liver cancer—are increasing at an alarming rate in rural areas.
He said the government is giving highest importance to preventive measures, as prevention is preferable to relying solely on conventional treatment.
At the event, awards were presented to individual blood donors and various organizations involved in blood donation activities.
Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) Mayor Abdus Salam, Executive Director of Ziaur Rahman Foundation and cancer specialist Professor Dr Farhad Halim Donar also spoke on the occasion while BTS President Engineer MA Matin was in the chair.
Professor Dr Harun Al Rashid, President of the Doctors Association of Bangladesh (DAB), and Engineer Riazul Islam, Chairman of the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (RAJUK) were also present.

item.description:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Friday that they had struck two tankers attempting to pass though the strategic Strait of Hormuz under the “air escort” of the US military.
The IRGC said the “non-compliant oil tankers... were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions.”
The Guards said the tankers had attempted to pass the strait via “an undeclared route,” the US-backed alternative to Tehran’s designated waterway closer to its own shores.
Iran has effectively maintained control over navigation through Hormuz since the outbreak of the war on February 28, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the waterway.
On Thursday, the Guards said two oil tankers attempting to transit the Strait had turned back after one caught fire.

43% of Aman seedling transplantation completed in Rangpur region
item.description:
Aman rice transplantation has been completed on 43% of the target farmland in the Rangpur agricultural region, with farmers continuing planting in full swing amid favourable monsoon rainfall.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), Aman seedlings have so far been transplanted on 267,267 hectares of land out of the targeted 621,550 hectares across the region.
Md Shirajul Islam, additional director of the DAE for Rangpur region, expressed optimism that the cultivation target would be achieved this season as weather conditions remain favourable.
The DAE has set a production target of 2.01 million tonnes of clean Aman rice (3.01 million tonnes in paddy equivalent) from 621,550 hectares across Rangpur, Gaibandha, Kurigram, Lalmonirhat and Nilphamari districts.
The target includes 1.67 million tonnes of high-yielding Aman rice from 524,520 hectares, 314,221 tonnes of hybrid Aman rice from 86,020 hectares, and 20,737 tonnes of local Aman rice from 11,010 hectares.
Last season, farmers produced 2.00 million tonnes of clean Aman rice from 616,299 hectares in the region.
Farmers have prepared seedbeds on 34,586 hectares—13.77% more than the required 30,401 hectares—to ensure an adequate supply of seedlings.
The government, through the DAE, has distributed quality Aman seeds and fertilisers among small and marginal farmers. Authorities have also prepared contingency plans, including late-variety and floating seedbeds, to address any seedling shortages in the event of flooding in August.
"We have instructed field-level agricultural officers to provide all necessary support and modern technologies to ensure successful Aman cultivation this season," Shirajul Islam said.
Farmers across Sadar, Gangachara, Taraganj, Mithapukur and Pirgachha upazilas said transplantation had gained momentum following frequent seasonal rainfall.
"We are hopeful of achieving the Aman cultivation target this season," said farmer Mofizar Rahman of Taraganj.
Another farmer, Anwar Hossain of Gangachara, said the young Aman plants were growing well due to the recent rains.

item.title: August may mark peak of Bangladesh's dengue season
item.description:
Public health experts have warned that Bangladesh's dengue situation could worsen significantly from August as persistent monsoon rainfall creates ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, with infections and deaths already surging sharply in July.
The warning comes as official data shows a sharp rise in both infections and fatalities compared with the first half of the year, raising concerns that the country is entering the peak dengue season.
During the first six months of this year, 18 people died from dengue. In just the first 30 days of July, however, the death toll reached 35—almost double the number recorded during the previous six months combined.
The infection trend is equally alarming. Between January and June, Bangladesh recorded 6,104 dengue cases. In July alone, infections climbed to 9,053. According to the latest figures, the country has reported 15,153 dengue cases and 53 deaths so far this year.
Health experts say July's sharp increase signals the beginning of the annual dengue peak, which typically extends through August and September. This year, however, favorable weather conditions and the expanding distribution of Aedes mosquitoes could prolong the outbreak into October.
Persistent rainfall throughout July has left stagnant water across cities, municipalities and rural areas, creating ideal breeding sites for Aedes mosquitoes. Rooftops, under-construction buildings, flowerpots, discarded tires, drums, buckets and other open containers have all become potential sources of mosquito breeding.
Professor Kabirul Bashar, an entomologist at the Department of Zoology at Jahangirnagar University, told Dhaka Tribune: "Recent rainfall has created highly favorable breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. As a result, dengue infections are likely to increase further in August. However, the number of deaths will largely depend on how quickly patients seek treatment and are admitted to hospitals."
Experts say widespread stagnant water left by monsoon rains has significantly expanded Aedes breeding sites, accelerating transmission. While Aedes mosquitoes were once believed to breed only in clean water, recent research suggests they can also reproduce in semi-polluted or contaminated water, putting many previously overlooked locations at risk.
Weather conditions have further compounded the problem. Heavy rainfall early in July, followed by rising temperatures and subsequent rain, has created an ideal environment for rapid mosquito reproduction.
The density of Aedes mosquito larvae is reportedly higher across much of the country than it was at the same time last year. Experts identify Dhaka, Chittagong and Barisal divisions as particularly vulnerable, while warning of rising infections in Cox's Bazar, Comilla, Chandpur, Gazipur, Narsingdi, Mymensingh, Manikganj, Munshiganj, Narayanganj, Khulna and Bagerhat.
Barisal Division recorded the highest number of dengue cases last year, and a similar trend is emerging this year. At the same time, Dhaka continues to account for a significant share of infections and deaths.
Dengue, once largely confined to the capital, has spread to nearly every division of the country over the past several years. Increased human mobility, rapid urbanization and the wider distribution of Aedes mosquitoes have placed district and upazila towns at growing risk.
The rapid spread outside Dhaka is also placing additional pressure on healthcare services. Many district hospitals lack specialized dengue treatment facilities and adequate diagnostic capacity, making severe cases more difficult to manage.
Another growing concern this year is the changing distribution of dengue virus serotypes. Recent surveillance indicates that the DENV-3 serotype has become increasingly dominant.
Doctors warn that people previously infected with one dengue serotype face a greater risk of developing severe dengue if they become infected with a different serotype, raising concerns that the number of critical cases could increase in the coming months.
Hospitals across the country are already admitting increasing numbers of dengue patients daily. Many arrive with high fever, severe body aches, headaches, vomiting, weakness and declining platelet counts.
Doctors say many patients initially mistake dengue for a common viral fever, delaying treatment and increasing the risk of complications. They advise anyone with a fever lasting more than three days or showing symptoms consistent with dengue to seek medical attention promptly and undergo testing without delay.
Despite significant spending on dengue control every year, experts say prevention efforts continue to fall short. In many cases, mosquito control campaigns focus on areas with relatively limited Aedes breeding, while rooftops, basements, construction sites, flowerpots, water tanks, drums and discarded containers—where stagnant water commonly accumulates—receive insufficient attention.
Experts also stress that fogging alone cannot effectively control dengue. Eliminating breeding sites and destroying mosquito larvae remain the most effective ways to reduce mosquito populations.
Professor Bashar said: "To keep the situation under control, authorities must strengthen efforts to control both larvae and adult mosquitoes simultaneously. Vector control activities must also continue consistently. Sporadic or seasonal campaigns alone cannot contain dengue."
He emphasized that preventing Aedes breeding remains the most effective defense against dengue. Water should not be allowed to remain stagnant for more than three days in or around homes, while flowerpots, air-conditioner trays, drums, buckets, discarded tires and water collected at construction sites should be cleaned regularly.
Experts also urge people not to ignore fever symptoms. Anyone developing a fever should seek medical advice promptly, stay well hydrated and undergo dengue testing if necessary. Protective measures against mosquito bites should be maintained even during the daytime, when Aedes mosquitoes are most active.
Based on current infection trends, rising fatalities, prevailing weather conditions and the expanding distribution of Aedes mosquitoes, public health experts believe August will be the most critical month of this year's dengue season. Without sustained vector control, rapid diagnosis and public participation in eliminating breeding sites, infections could rise further in September and the outbreak may continue into October.
They say dengue is no longer solely a healthcare issue but a broader public health challenge linked to urban management, environmental conditions, local government performance and public awareness. Alongside coordinated government action, active public participation will be essential to prevent the situation from deteriorating further.

item.title: Bangladesh’s 54 prisons lack ambulances as healthcare crisis deepens
item.description:
Deaths in police and prison custody continue to raise serious concerns in Bangladesh, with human rights groups questioning the treatment of detainees and prison authorities themselves acknowledging severe deficiencies in healthcare services.
The crisis extends beyond allegations of custodial abuse. Prison officials say none of the country's 54 prisons has an ambulance, many prison doctors fail to remain on duty, and costly medical equipment has sat unused for years due to staff shortages.
According to the human rights organization Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), at least 61 people died in prison custody and four in police custody during the first six months of this year. In 2025, the organization recorded 116 deaths in prison custody and at least 11 in police custody.
Responding to concerns over custodial deaths, Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, additional commissioner of the Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police, told Dhaka Tribune that no such incidents had occurred recently in Dhaka. He said Police Headquarters has been actively addressing the issue and that action is taken whenever police personnel are found guilty of misconduct.
AIG (Media and Public Relations) HM Shahadat Hossain of Police Headquarters said ensuring the safety and legal rights of everyone in police custody is the force's responsibility. He said existing laws, court directives and standard operating procedures (SOPs) are being strictly followed, while allegations of negligence or misconduct are investigated and legal action taken where appropriate.
The Department of Prisons admits that inadequate healthcare remains one of the biggest challenges facing Bangladesh's prison system.
Officials said none of the country's 54 prisons has an ambulance. Prisoners requiring emergency treatment are transported to hospitals in pickup vans or locally known "Laguna" vehicles. Authorities acknowledged that some inmates die en route because oxygen support is unavailable and treatment is delayed.
Although each of Bangladesh's 75 prisons is supposed to have two full-time doctors, officials said many physicians neither report regularly nor remain on duty throughout the day, disrupting healthcare services and delaying treatment.
The department also revealed that modern diagnostic and treatment equipment purchased nearly a decade ago for the 200-bed Kashimpur Prison Hospital has never been used because of a lack of trained personnel.
Several recently released prisoners told Dhaka Tribune that proper medical care is virtually nonexistent inside prisons. They said doctors are rarely available and that delays caused by the lack of ambulances often prove fatal.
Former inmates also alleged they witnessed prisoners suffering from heart disease, chest pain and other serious illnesses die before reaching hospital. They further claimed negligence had led to miscarriages among female prisoners.
According to the Department of Prisons, 129 inmates died in prisons across Bangladesh during the past six months, including 74 who died before they could be transported to hospital.
(The Department of Prisons' figure includes all inmate deaths during the period, while ASK's statistics are based on its own monitoring of custodial deaths.)
Assistant Inspector General of Prisons (Development) Md Jannat-ul-Farhad told Dhaka Tribune that requests for ambulances for all 54 prisons had remained pending for years.
"Discussions have been held with the ministry, but there is still no certainty about when ambulances will be provided," he said.
Farhad said every prison is supposed to have two doctors providing round-the-clock medical care, but many physicians neither report regularly nor remain on duty throughout the day, leaving inmates without timely treatment.
He said the lack of ambulances forces prison authorities to transport critically ill inmates in unsuitable vehicles, with some dying before reaching hospital.
Farhad also said much of the expensive medical equipment has deteriorated after years of lying unused.
"We have a 200-bed prison hospital in Kashimpur equipped with all the necessary modern machines," he said. "However, those machines have remained unopened for almost 10 years. We have operating theatre equipment, X-ray machines and many advanced medical devices, but we cannot use them because we simply do not have the required manpower."
He added that an X-ray machine purchased for Chittagong Prison Hospital nearly a decade ago has also never been commissioned.
On July 30, Mizanur Rahman, 55, who had been arrested in connection with an attempted rape case involving a seven-year-old child in Faridganj, Chandpur, died after falling ill in police custody.
On June 24, Nurul Alam, a leader of the banned Jubo League, died in Chittagong prison custody. He had reportedly been arrested in good health just a day earlier.
Three days earlier, on June 21, Mirza Ishtiaq Ahmed Pranto, an activist of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, died while in the custody of the Detective Branch in Faridpur. His family alleged he was beaten in front of his mother during his arrest and received his body the following day.
Another widely discussed incident occurred on January 31 last year, when Touhidul Islam, a Jubo Dal leader, died while in the custody of a joint security force in Cumilla. Images showing apparent signs of torture on his body later circulated on social media.
Families of victims have consistently alleged that their relatives were taken into custody in good health but later died after being tortured. Authorities have rejected such allegations in several cases, citing illness or other causes.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Thursday, human rights activist Nur Khan Liton said law enforcement agencies in Bangladesh have long operated with a sense of impunity.
"Police often believe they are above the law and can do whatever they want. They have little regard for legal procedures."
Referring to the death of Mirza Ishtiaq Ahmed Pranto, Liton said video footage of the arrest appeared to show detectives striking him around the head and ears while several officers restrained him.
Liton alleged that Pranto sustained severe injuries during the arrest and claimed those injuries ultimately led to his death in police custody.
He also recalled an earlier incident at Khulna Sadar Police Station during the previous government's tenure in which a Chhatra Dal activist was allegedly suspended and beaten inside the station. After footage of the incident went viral, the officers involved were transferred elsewhere, he said.
Liton said the practice of temporarily suspending or transferring officers accused of abuse was itself a serious problem.
"Police officers involved in these crimes should be dismissed from the force and prosecuted under criminal law."
He added: "The death of a person in state custody should never be treated as an ordinary or natural death. Only exemplary punishment through due legal process can deter such crimes."
Supreme Court senior lawyer Saeed Ahmed Raja told Dhaka Tribune that whenever a person dies in custody, authorities may conduct an inquest, a post-mortem examination and, where necessary, a judicial or magistrate-led investigation. Courts may also order an independent inquiry.
"If there are allegations of torture, a separate criminal case can be filed under the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention) Act, 2013," he said.
However, Raja noted that such cases face significant challenges.
"To date, there has been no successful conviction in Bangladesh under this law."
Asked about the obstacles, Raja said proving custodial torture generally requires physical evidence of injuries, medical reports, eyewitness testimony, information about the time and place of the alleged abuse, and evidence that any confession or statement was obtained through coercion.
"In most cases, victims or their families are unable to produce sufficient evidence. As a result, these cases rarely lead to convictions."
Raja also pointed to a broader due process concern.
"In many other countries, when someone is taken into police custody, officers first ask whether the detainee has a lawyer. In Bangladesh, however, it often takes considerable time before family members or lawyers can determine where a detainee is being held."

item.title: Yasser: Media must act responsibly to curb AI-driven misinformation
item.description:
Yasser Khan Chowdhury is one of the emerging faces of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). Bringing years of experience in the information technology sector into politics, he now serves as state minister for information and broadcasting.
The son of former Mymensingh-9 lawmaker Anwarul Hossain Khan Chowdhury, he grew up in a political family but forged his own career in technology before entering public life. He held a senior position in the BBC's information technology division in London and previously worked at IBM.
A long-time BNP activist, he served as convener of Nandail Upazila BNP and as a senior member of the district unit. After being elected from Mymensingh-9 in the 2026 parliamentary election, he was appointed state minister for Information and Broadcasting. He also chairs the Journalist Welfare Trust.
In an interview with Dhaka Tribune Staff Reporter Tanvir Hasan, the state minister discusses media freedom, misinformation, digital governance, and the future of Bangladesh's media landscape.
The current government considers the media one of the pillars of democracy. We are committed to ensuring full media freedom. The government is working to ensure journalists can perform their professional responsibilities safely while protecting freedom of expression.
Efforts are also underway to reorganize the Media Reform Commission and strengthen professionalism across the media.
Investigative journalism and corruption reporting often face legal challenges. What is the government's position on this issue?
So far, the government has not pressured any media outlet to withdraw a report or attempted to control the media. You could say this has been our biggest decision.
Under the previous fascist regime, reports were withdrawn under various forms of pressure whenever they went against the government or government officials.
We believe journalists are among the government's strongest partners in combating corruption.
Government officials have been instructed to avoid unnecessary delays in providing information. We are also considering whether they should receive specialized training on this issue.
To improve transparency, every government office is now required to regularly update its website with administrative and financial information. As a result, journalists and members of the public can obtain information simply by searching those websites.
We will also consult stakeholders to determine whether additional steps can be taken to make journalists' work easier.
What monitoring mechanisms is the ministry using to prevent rumors and misinformation from spreading through social media and online platforms?
The Press Institute Bangladesh (PIB), under the Ministry of Information, has launched a fact-checking initiative called BanglaFact. Several private fact-checking platforms have also emerged.
However, the misuse of artificial intelligence is becoming an increasing concern. AI is being used to create manipulated images, videos, and false information, which many people share without realizing they are fake.
The media has a vital role to play in addressing this challenge. News organizations must avoid using information from social media without proper verification. That will further strengthen the credibility of the media.
Discussions are underway on a balanced Digital and Social Media Framework for social media and digital platforms.
Our objective is not to impose censorship. Rather, we want to promote responsible and decent behavior while upholding journalistic ethics.
A number of reforms are being introduced at Bangladesh Television and Bangladesh Betar to better reflect the interests and expectations of audiences across generations.
Measures are being taken to improve the quality of dramas, entertainment programs, documentaries, and news broadcasts to encourage more people to watch and listen.
We have also initiated forensic audits of both organizations so the public can see the true extent of the looting that took place in the past.
As you know, nearly Tk100 crore was spent to broadcast the previous FIFA World Cup on BTV. That was a project of looting. Now, under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, with a people's government in place, we have been able to broadcast this World Cup free of charge. That is the difference between an authoritarian government and one that is accountable to the people. It is your responsibility to communicate these facts properly to the public.
We are considering modernizing the Press Council to help maintain standards among registered news portals. The proposal is being discussed with stakeholders before any decision is made.
We are also working to create a database of genuine journalists to curb fake journalism, while encouraging media organizations to implement the Wage Board or an appropriate salary structure for journalists.
What support is the government providing to expand Bangladesh's film industry globally and modernize cinema halls across the country?
Initiatives have already been taken to overhaul the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation (FDC). Long-overdue payments owed to FDC employees have begun to be cleared.
Renovation and construction work at both the FDC and Kabirpur Film City are now in full swing, helping restore momentum to the country's film industry.
Special initiatives have also been taken to renovate cinema halls, build new multiplexes, and install modern screening facilities.
Before independence, the media was one of the principal instruments of the national liberation struggle. After independence, its primary responsibility has been to institutionalize democracy and ensure transparency in government.
The media's role has expanded over time. However, the digital age has also created new challenges in maintaining quality, and overcoming those challenges is now our goal.
The main weaknesses are language barriers and the lack of globally focused content. We still produce too little English-language content that meets international standards, and there is a shortage of analysis and presentation tailored to global audiences.
There is also a lack of world-class technology and in-depth investigative journalism. Moreover, the long-term professional investment required to build an internationally recognized news organization has not yet been made.
Maintaining a balance between protecting media freedom and preserving discipline in state administration is something every responsible government must practice.
As a matter of principle, our party believes in media freedom. From the government of martyred President Ziaur Rahman to the government of the late Begum Khaleda Zia and the current government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, every BNP government has upheld media freedom.
Certainly, it is not about words. What matters is how it is reflected in practice.
A television channel has alleged that one of its reports disappeared after objections from a state minister. How do you respond?
If there are allegations that a report disappeared because of a state minister or that a media organization was pressured, that is extremely unfortunate.
The current government does not support suppressing the media to protect any individual's personal interests.
I believe it is essential to strengthen journalists' financial and professional security, improve professional and ethical standards, enhance the powers of the Press Council, and stop the spread of misinformation and disinformation.
The media should also remain free from partisan influence and operate under an independent oversight framework.
The government is working to prevent the misuse of the ICT Act and cyber security laws.
We are discussing with the Ministry of Home Affairs the introduction of a special screening and preliminary investigation mechanism so journalists are not unnecessarily subjected to legal complications or arrested without proper review.
Since the current government assumed office, no journalist has been charged under the ICT Act.
Thank you.
Thank you, and thanks to all the readers of Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Study finds 54,000 microplastics per liter in soybean oil sold in Bangladesh
item.description:
Soybean oil sold in Bangladesh contains alarming levels of microplastic contamination, with researchers detecting an average of nearly 54,000 plastic particles per liter in both branded and loose varieties, according to a new study.
The findings, published in the April 2026 issue of the peer-reviewed Journal of Food Composition and Analysis , raise fresh concerns about food safety and the long-term public health impacts of microplastic exposure.
The study, conducted jointly by researchers from Jahangirnagar University (JU) and Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP), found that loose soybean oil contains significantly higher levels of microplastics than bottled oil.
Researchers say it is the first scientific investigation into microplastic contamination in edible oil in Bangladesh and the first globally to identify polyurethane (PU) and nylon microplastics in edible oil.
The researchers found an average of 53,922 (±10,510) microplastic particles per liter in soybean oil samples collected from markets in Dhaka.
Loose soybean oil contained an average of 59,778 particles per liter, compared with 48,067 particles in bottled oil, making contamination in loose oil about 1.24 times higher.
The highest contamination level was recorded in a loose oil sample collected from Tejgaon, where researchers detected 70,467 microplastic particles per liter.
The researchers believe the higher contamination may be linked to Tejgaon's concentration of plastic and textile industries, airborne synthetic fibers, repeated use of plastic storage containers, and exposure to open environments during storage and sale.
How the study was conducted
The researchers collected 60 one-liter soybean oil samples comprising three branded (bottled) and three non-branded (loose) varieties from supermarkets and open markets in Tejgaon, Uttara, and Dhaka Cantonment.
The samples were divided into six categories. Ten samples from each category were combined into a composite sample, producing six composite samples for laboratory analysis.
Each composite sample was analyzed three times using solvent dilution, stereo microscopy, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the findings.
Lead researcher Prof Shafi Mohammad Tareq of JU's Department of Environmental Sciences told Dhaka Tribune that the team analyzed both branded and loose soybean oil available in Dhaka's markets.
"Our analysis found thousands of microplastic particles per liter in both types of oil, with fibers and fragments accounting for the majority of the contamination," he said.
Six types of plastic identified
The study identified six polymer types in the oil samples: low-density polyethylene (LDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polypropylene (PP), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyurethane (PU), and nylon.
The detection of polyurethane and nylon is particularly significant, as the researchers say these polymers have never before been reported in edible oil.
They believe polyurethane may originate from industrial coatings and adhesives, while nylon could enter oil through filters, nets, or manufacturing equipment.
More than 82% of the detected microplastics were fibers, while fragments accounted for nearly 10%. Transparent particles were the most common, representing more than 56% of the total. Most particles measured between 101 and 500 micrometers.
Children face the greatest exposure risk
The researchers also carried out a Human Exposure Assessment to estimate how many microplastic particles people could ingest through regular soybean oil consumption.
The estimates were based on average soybean oil consumption in Bangladesh, assuming an average adult body weight of 70kg and a child's average weight of 16kg.
According to the assessment, an adult could ingest an average of 17.65 microplastic particles a day through soybean oil alone. This amounts to about 6,441 particles a year and an estimated 477,000 particles over a lifetime.
The potential exposure is considerably higher for children because of their lower body weight. The study estimates that a child could ingest an average of 77.21 microplastic particles daily, about 28,180 annually, and nearly 2.09 million particles over a lifetime.
The researchers cautioned that these figures are model-based estimates rather than direct measurements of microplastics in the human body.
Public health concerns
Prof Tareq said microplastics are increasingly regarded as an "emerging contaminant" with potentially serious long-term health implications.
"Microplastics can enter edible oil during production, processing, transportation, storage, and packaging," he said.
He added that plastic pipes, filters, seals, and packaging materials used throughout the supply chain are among the likely sources of contamination.
The study notes that previous research has linked long-term ingestion of microplastics to digestive disorders, inflammation, cellular damage, hormonal disruption, metabolic disorders, and reproductive health concerns.
It also notes that particles smaller than 130 micrometers may cross biological barriers and enter the bloodstream, although scientists say more research is needed to fully understand their long-term health effects in humans.
Public health expert Dr Shamsur Rahman described microplastics as an emerging public health challenge.
He said studies around the world have detected microplastics in the human brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, stomach, testes, and ovaries.
"Harmful chemicals attached to these particles may increase cancer risks and damage vital organs, including the liver and kidneys," he said.
Regulatory gaps
The researchers say Bangladesh currently lacks national standards or routine monitoring systems for microplastic contamination in food products.
As a result, they say reliable national data on contamination levels, exposure pathways, and long-term health impacts remain limited.
Dr Rahman said stricter quality control is needed throughout the food supply chain, along with modern laboratories and stronger government oversight to regularly monitor microplastic contamination in food.
Although all six sample groups fell within the "moderate pollution" category under the study's Microplastic Pollution Index (MPI), the researchers cautioned that the index is intended only to compare contamination levels between samples and should not be interpreted as an official food safety standard.
Recommendations
The researchers called for coordinated national action to reduce microplastic contamination throughout the edible oil supply chain.
They recommended strengthening quality control during production and refining, replacing plastic equipment with safer alternatives where possible, tightening oversight of loose oil storage and sales, introducing national monitoring standards for microplastics in food, investing in laboratory capacity, and expanding plastic waste management and recycling programs.
"Simply raising public awareness will not be enough," Prof Tareq said.
"Producers, regulators, and policymakers must work together to identify and reduce contamination sources from production to consumers' tables. Without coordinated action, the health and economic consequences of microplastic pollution could become much more severe in the future."

item.title: Where shadows began: Inside the crumbling birthplace of British India's celluloid pioneer
item.description:
The last mile was not motorable. I disembarked from the car and walked a rural path under an overcast midday sky. My shadow shrank to its minimum length, pooling tightly around my feet. Walking deep into Bakjuri village in Manikganj last Monday, my faint shadow mimicked my actual width without stretching. As I moved, it looked as though I were stepping on a small, dark puddle of my own shape.
The interplay of light and shadows had captivated a young boy in this very village some 150 years ago.
This structure is a powerful testament to history being reclaimed by nature. Over decades of abandonment, a massive banyan tree has grown directly over and through the old brick house—the birthplace and childhood home of Hiralal Sen. Photo: Collected/ Dhaka Tribune
Born into an affluent Zamindar family, he used to project shadow puppets onto the wall using his palms and fingers. Unsurprisingly, this boy would eventually emerge as the visionary who established British India’s first indigenous film production house—the Royal Bioscope Company—and became the subcontinent's first filmmaker. His name was Hiralal Sen.
The dirt pathway led me through his ancestral roots. The village path, lined with lush green vegetation, was cluttered with sand-dredging pipes for road development, making the trek somewhat hazardous. After a 15-minute walk, I reached Bakjuri Government Primary School. The building that houses the school, established in 1960, is named after Hiralal Sen.
Inside, teachers Tulsi Rani Sarker, Sharmin Akhter, and their colleagues greeted me. They confirmed that the school compound, the adjacent playfield, and the pond were all once part of Hiralal’s ancestral estate.
With the midday school break approaching, I took a few photographs, bade farewell to the teachers and students, and asked for a guide to the remnants of Hiralal’s home. Three children led me to the far bank of the pond. There lay a ruined structure, largely obscured by the creepers of a massive banyan tree. Over decades of abandonment, the tree had grown directly through the old brick house. Its thick, invasive aerial roots wrapped tightly around the colonial-era brickwork like a protective cage.
While many villagers today identify the structure—now just a fragment of a larger ruin—as an ancient temple, others maintain it is the remains of Hiralal’s ancestral home.
Hiralal Sen Photo: Collected/ Dhaka Tribune
Locals warn of snakes, making it too dangerous to enter. Yet, one can still glimpse hints of the decorative archway over the lower doors and windows, even though the masonry is heavily cracked and supported almost entirely by the roots. This was the site Hiralal Sen once called home.
Born on August 2, 1866, Hiralal Sen is recognized by historians as the premier filmmaker of the Indian subcontinent. Long before modern studios existed, he was producing short films, documentaries, and advertisements. His father, Chandra Mohan Sen, was an eminent lawyer who practiced at the Dhaka District Court and later transitioned to the Calcutta High Court, raising his family in Kolkata.
While still a student in Manikganj and later at Dhaka Collegiate School, Hiralal helped found the Amravati Fine Arts Association and established Bengal’s first photography studio, "Hiralal and Brothers," in Bakjuri.
A rural dirt pathway leads through the ancestral roots of Hiralal Sen in Bakjuri. Lined with lush green trees, the path has long been cluttered with sand-dredging pipes for road development work that moves at a snail’s pace. Photo: Collected/ Dhaka Tribune
In 1898, a film troupe en route to Paris screened one Mr Stevenson's short film alongside the stage show The Flower of Persia at Calcutta's Star Theatre. Borrowing Stevenson's camera, Sen filmed "A Dancing Scene" from the opera. He then secured funds from his parents to purchase his own cinematograph camera from London, launching the Royal Bioscope Company that same year.
In a creative career spanning until 1913, Sen made over forty short films. Most captured theatrical productions at Amarendra Dutta's Classic Theatre in Calcutta. His longest film, the 1903 production Alibaba and the Forty Thieves, was also based on a Classic Theatre performance. Sen was also a regional pioneer in advertising films, directing promotional shorts for Jabakusum Hair Oil and Edwards Tonic.
Recently, I watched the biopic Hiralal, directed by Arun Roy. The film beautifully captures the artist’s dedication, his creations, and his personal traumas. In one poignant scene, the Calcutta police raid his house and confiscate a film reel to prevent a public screening. This incident highlights Sen's role as a political cinema pioneer; he had documented an anti-partition demonstration and anti-colonial rally at the Calcutta Town Hall on September 22, 1905.
The writer, along with a group of teachers and students, stands in front of the Bakjuri Government Primary School. The building is named after Hiralal Sen, recognized by historians as the very first filmmaker of the Indian subcontinent. Photo: Collected/ Dhaka Tribune
The Royal Bioscope Company produced its final film in 1913. Sen’s poor business acumen caused the company to fold, and a mysterious warehouse fire subsequently destroyed his entire life's work. A cancer diagnosis led to his premature death in 1917.
Long after his passing, historians debated who held the definitive title of the subcontinent's first filmmaker: Hiralal Sen of Bangladesh or Dadasaheb Phalke of Maharashtra, India. This debate is unnecessary when looking at the facts. Hiralal Sen was the first to capture a movie in British India with his 1903 theatrical filming of Alibaba and the Forty Thieves. Dadasaheb Phalke was the first to make a full-length, narrative feature film, releasing Raja Harishchandra several years later in 1913. Both remain monumental pioneers of cinema in colonial-era India.

item.description:
At least 18 Rohingyas were rescued alive after a boat carrying people fleeing Myanmar capsized in the sea off Teknaf while attempting to enter Bangladesh on Friday morning, with many others still reported missing.
The incident occurred around 12:00pm near the boat jetty at Poschim para of Shah Porir Dwip in Subrang union under Teknaf upazila.
The rescued Rohingyas were handed over to the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB).
Md Ismail, Local fisherman, said they managed to rescue 18 people after the boat sank but many others remain missing. He said none of those rescued were women or children.
Lt Col Hanifur Rahman Bhuiyan, Commanding Officer of Teknaf-2 BGB Battalion, said 18 Rohingyas had been rescued following the boat capsize near Shah Porir Dwip and are now in BGB custody.
He said authorities are verifying the reasons behind their entry into Bangladesh, after which necessary legal steps will be taken.
